Prologue

The Accidental Intactivist's Inquiry

★ From the Lead Researcher
A LETTER · READ FIRST

My name is Tone Pettit. If you are an American man reading this, there is a high probability your parents made a decision when you were an infant to remove a portion of your genital skin.

For most men, this was framed strictly as a prophylactic hygiene measure. It was so normalized that questioning it often feels taboo.

By a conscious choice of my parents in the 1970s, I grew up intact. I was an outlier in a culture where routine infant circumcision was the unquestioned, 90% norm. I became an "accidental intactivist," a witness to an alteration that nearly all my peers had undergone without a say.

If someone asked you honestly how you felt about your circumcision status, what would you say?

That is the question I set out to ask when I built this anonymous survey. The biology of the foreskin is well understood. Its nerve density, mechanical function, and immunological role are documented in anatomy textbooks. Yet routine infant circumcision became standard practice in America during an era when self-pleasure was treated as a medical disorder. The procedure was designed to reduce sexual sensation.

Now the culture is shifting. Newborn circumcision rates in the United States have fallen below 50% for the first time in over a century. Parents are asking questions that went unasked a generation ago.

Survey recruitment flyers, 2024
Grassroots Outreach

There was no advertising budget or clinical recruitment pipeline. The survey spread entirely through grassroots efforts. It was posted to forums, shared across social media, and passed hand to hand. Five hundred people showed up to answer anonymously.

This project exists to invite you to pay attention to what surfaces when people are given the space to share their experiences honestly. What follows is a guided tour through their answers, summarized and never argued. Where I editorialize, it is clearly labeled. Otherwise, we simply report what they said.

Tone Pettit
The Accidental Intactivist · Lead Researcher · Seattle
Act I

The Mechanical Reality

Does removing the foreskin change the physics of sex?

To understand the impact, we first have to look at the mechanics. We asked every respondent to rate their sexual experience across six key metrics. The data reveals a stark, quantifiable "Pleasure Gap." On every single metric, intact men scored significantly higher.

This is not a subjective feeling. It is a mechanical failure.
The intact penis is a self-lubricating system with a natural gliding mechanism. When you remove that tissue, you convert a dynamic sensory organ into a dry, friction-based tool. The most dramatic drop was in "Pleasure from Mobile Skin," where circumcised men reported a 55% reduction in satisfaction.

Act II

The Emotional Fallout

The "Harmless Snip" Myth Collapses.

The defining myth of infant circumcision is that because they are babies, they won't remember it, and therefore they won't care. When you give men an anonymous space to speak, that myth shatters.
★ Gratitude vs. Regret
EXHIBIT 02 · RESENTMENT MIRROR
Our data shows that over 86% of infant-circumcised respondents experience frequent feelings of resentment, loss, anger, or grief regarding the non-consensual alteration of their bodies. They are living with a permanent reduction in their sensory potential, chosen for them before they could even speak.

Act III

The Journey of Reclamation

Can the damage be undone?

The realization of this loss is so profound that a growing movement of men spend years actively "restoring" their foreskins through non-surgical tissue expansion. Our data validates their immense effort.

Restoring men report significant improvements in mobility, comfort, and the need for lubrication. But the data also reveals a tragic truth. While you can stretch skin to simulate the mechanics, you cannot regrow the thousands of specialized nerve endings that were amputated at birth. The original high-definition hardware is permanently gone.

The Resolution

Empowerment

The Cultural Spell is Breaking.

If parents were given this data on day one—if they knew the reality of the pleasure gap and the risk of lifelong resentment—would they still choose to alter their sons? We asked our 500 respondents what they would do if they had a son today.
★ The Convergence
EXHIBIT 14 · ALL COHORTS
433
Of 500 respondents, 433 flow to "Keep Intact."

The convergence is absolute. Even among the men who were cut themselves, the overwhelming majority refuse to perpetuate the practice on the next generation.

There is no medical justification for the routine removal of healthy, erogenous tissue from a non-consenting child. The decision belongs to the person who has to live in the body.

We are finally equipped with the data to break the cycle.

Further Exploration

The narrative above captures the core findings of the Accidental Intactivist survey. For those interested in the underlying demographics, cultural factors, and survey architecture, we have preserved the following detailed exhibits.

Now that you've seen who showed up and where they came from, here's how the survey actually worked. Below is the routing architecture — a single entry point, blinded experience questions first, then a fork into separate pathways. Understanding this structure is essential to trusting the data that follows.
